claim: Germ granules are protein-RNA condensates that segregate with the embryonic germline.
source: Germ granules are protein-RNA condensates that segregate with the embryonic germline.
evidence: This is a general statement about germ granules supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans embryos, germ (P) granule assembly requires MEG-3.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans embryos, germ (P) granule assembly requires MEG-3, an intrinsically disordered protein that forms RNA-rich condensates on the surface of PGL condensates at the core of P granules.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and cited previous work.

claim: MEG-3 is an intrinsically disordered protein that forms RNA-rich condensates on the surface of PGL condensates at the core of P granules.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans embryos, germ (P) granule assembly requires MEG-3, an intrinsically disordered protein that forms RNA-rich condensates on the surface of PGL condensates at the core of P granules.
evidence: This structural and functional characterization is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: MEG-3 is related to the GCNA family.
source: MEG-3 is related to the GCNA family and contains an N-terminal disordered region (IDR) and a predicted ordered C-terminus featuring an HMG-like motif (HMGL).
evidence: This relationship is supported by sequence analysis and comparison shown in Figure 1C.

claim: MEG-3 contains an N-terminal disordered region (IDR) and a predicted ordered C-terminus featuring an HMG-like motif (HMGL).
source: MEG-3 is related to the GCNA family and contains an N-terminal disordered region (IDR) and a predicted ordered C-terminus featuring an HMG-like motif (HMGL).
evidence: This structural prediction is supported by computational analysis (IUPred2A) and sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1.

claim: MEG-3 is a modular protein that uses its IDR to bind RNA and its C-terminus to drive condensation.
source: We find that MEG-3 is a modular protein that uses its IDR to bind RNA and its C-terminus to drive condensation.
evidence: This functional characterization is supported by in vitro binding assays and condensation experiments presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The HMGL motif mediates binding to PGL-3.
source: The HMGL motif mediates binding to PGL-3 and is required for co-assembly of MEG-3 and PGL-3 condensates in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down assays and bead halo assays shown in Figure 7.

claim: The HMGL motif is required for co-assembly of MEG-3 and PGL-3 condensates in vivo.
source: The HMGL motif mediates binding to PGL-3 and is required for co-assembly of MEG-3 and PGL-3 condensates in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo imaging of MEG-3HMGL- mutants shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mutations in HMGL cause MEG-3 and PGL-3 to form separate condensates that no longer co-segregate to the germline or recruit RNA.
source: Mutations in HMGL cause MEG-3 and PGL-3 to form separate condensates that no longer co-segregate to the germline or recruit RNA.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Protein-based condensation mechanisms and condensate-condensate interactions are important in the assembly of RNA-rich germ granules.
source: Our findings highlight the importance of protein-based condensation mechanisms and condensate-condensate interactions in the assembly of RNA-rich germ granules.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental results showing that protein interactions drive condensate assembly.

claim: Germ granules resemble liquid condensates that assemble by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS).
source: In recent years, much progress has been made in our understanding of stress granule assembly with the realization that stress granules resemble liquid condensates that assemble by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from recent literature in the field.

claim: LLPS is a thermodynamic process that causes interacting molecules to dynamically partition between a dense condensed phase and a more dilute phase.
source: LLPS is a thermodynamic process that causes interacting molecules to dynamically partition between a dense condensed phase and a more dilute phase (e.g., the cytoplasm) (Banani et al., 2017; Mitrea and Kriwacki, 2016).
evidence: This definition is supported by cited references providing theoretical background.

claim: Low-affinity-binding interactions, often involving disordered and RNA-binding domains, are sufficient to drive LLPS of proteins and RNA in reconstituted systems.
source: Low-affinity-binding interactions, often involving disordered and RNA-binding domains, are sufficient to drive LLPS of proteins and RNA in reconstituted systems (Lin et al., 2015; Molliex et al., 2015; Zagrovic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited experimental studies in reconstituted systems.

claim: RNA can phase separate in the absence of proteins in vitro.
source: The ability of RNA to phase separate in the absence of proteins in vitro has also been proposed to contribute to RNA granule assembly in vivo, especially in the case of stress granules, which arise under conditions of general translational arrest (Tauber et al., 2020; Van Treeck et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited in vitro studies.

claim: Germ granules are not well-mixed, single-phase liquid droplets.
source: Unlike the dynamic condensates assembled by LLPS in vitro, germ granules are not well-mixed, single-phase liquid droplets.
evidence: This is supported by high-resolution microscopy observations cited in the text.

claim: Germ granules are heterogenous assemblies of dynamic and less dynamic condensates that co-assemble but do not fully mix.
source: High-resolution microscopy has revealed that germ granules are heterogenous assemblies of dynamic and less dynamic condensates that co-assemble but do not fully mix.
evidence: This is supported by cited microscopy studies.

claim: Drosophila germ granules contain non-dynamic RNA clusters embedded in dynamic, protein-rich condensates.
source: For example, Drosophila germ granules contain non-dynamic RNA clusters embedded in dynamic, protein-rich condensates (Little et al., 2015; Niepielko et al., 2018; Trcek et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on Drosophila germ granules.

claim: Germ granules in zebrafish and Xenopus are built on an amyloid-like scaffold that organizes mRNAs in nonoverlapping, transcript-specific zones.
source: Germ granules in zebrafish and Xenopus are built on an amyloid-like scaffold that organizes mRNAs in nonoverlapping, transcript-specific zones (Boke et al., 2016; Fuentes et al., 2018; Roovers et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on zebrafish and Xenopus germ granules.

claim: At the core of P granules are liquid condensates assembled by PGL proteins.
source: At the core of P granules are liquid condensates assembled by PGL proteins.
evidence: This is supported by previous studies and data in the manuscript.

claim: PGL-1 and PGL-3 are self-dimerizing, RGG domain proteins that readily form condensates able to recruit other P granule components, such as the VASA-related RNA helicase GLH-1.
source: PGL-1 and PGL-3 are self-dimerizing, RGG domain proteins that readily form condensates able to recruit other P granule components, such as the VASA-related RNA helicase GLH-1 (Aoki et al., 2016; Hanazawa et al., 2011; Saha et al., 2016; Updike et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies characterizing PGL proteins.

claim: PGL condensates exist in germ cells throughout oogenesis and are maternally inherited by the embryo.
source: PGL condensates exist in germ cells throughout oogenesis and are maternally inherited by the embryo.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about PGL condensates in C. elegans.

claim: In newly fertilized zygotes, the surface of PGL condensates becomes covered by smaller condensates assembled by MEG-3 and MEG-4.
source: In newly fertilized zygotes, the surface of PGL condensates becomes covered by smaller condensates assembled by MEG-3 and MEG-4, two homologous intrinsically disordered proteins (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited previous work.

claim: MEG-3 and MEG-4 are two homologous intrinsically disordered proteins.
source: In newly fertilized zygotes, the surface of PGL condensates becomes covered by smaller condensates assembled by MEG-3 and MEG-4, two homologous intrinsically disordered proteins (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and cited work.

claim: MEG-3 condensates resist dilution and salt challenge, consistent with a gel-like material.
source: Unlike PGL condensates, MEG-3 condensates resist dilution and salt challenge, consistent with a gel-like material (Putnam et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited experimental characterization.

claim: During zygote polarization, MEG-3 and MEG-4 condensates enrich with other germ plasm components in the posterior cytoplasm.
source: During zygote polarization, MEG-3 and MEG-4 condensates enrich with other germ plasm components in the posterior cytoplasm (Putnam et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies and data in the manuscript.

claim: Enrichment of MEG-3 and MEG-4 condensates in the posterior correlates with preferential growth of MEG-coated PGL droplets in the posterior and dissolution of 'naked' PGL droplets in the anterior side.
source: This relocalization correlates with preferential growth of MEG-coated PGL droplets in the posterior and dissolution of 'naked' PGL droplets in the anterior side (Brangwynne et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This correlation is supported by cited observations.

claim: P granules concentrate specific maternal transcripts.
source: In addition to PGL and MEG co-assemblies, P granules also concentrate specific maternal transcripts (Parker et al., 2020; Seydoux and Fire, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: MEG-3 is most directly responsible for recruiting mRNAs to P granules.
source: A survey of mRNAs that immunoprecipitate with PGL-1 and MEG-3 suggests that MEG-3 is most directly responsible for recruiting mRNAs to P granules (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited immunoprecipitation data.

claim: MEG-3 binds to ~500 maternal mRNAs, including transcripts coding for germline determinants.
source: MEG-3 binds to ~500 maternal mRNAs, including transcripts coding for germline determinants.
evidence: This is supported by cited RNA immunoprecipitation studies.

claim: Recruitment of mRNAs to P granules ensures their preferential segregation to the primordial germ cells.
source: Recruitment of mRNAs to P granules ensures their preferential segregation to the primordial germ cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the function of P granules in germline specification.

claim: Embryos lacking MEG-3 and MEG-4 do not localize PGL droplets, do not condense P granule-associated mRNAs, and display partially penetrant (30%) sterility.
source: Embryos lacking MEG-3 and MEG-4 do not localize PGL droplets, do not condense P granule-associated mRNAs, and display partially penetrant (30%) sterility (Lee et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited genetic studies and data in the manuscript.

claim: IUPred2A predicts in the MEG-3 sequence a N-terminal domain with high disorder and a C-terminal domain with lower disorder separated by a boundary region with mixed order/disorder (aa544–698).
source: IUPred2A (Mészáros et al., 2018) predicts in the MEG-3 sequence a N-terminal domain with high disorder and a C-terminal domain with lower disorder separated by a boundary region with mixed order/disorder (aa544–698) (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by computational prediction shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The MEG-3 C-terminus contains a predicted ordered 44 amino acid sequence (aa700–744) with homology to the HMG-like-fold found in the GCNA family of intrinsically disordered proteins.
source: The C-terminus contains a predicted ordered 44 amino acid sequence (aa700–744) with homology to the HMG-like-fold found in the GCNA family of intrinsically disordered proteins (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1C.

claim: GCNA family members contain long N-terminal disordered domains, but these do not share sequence homology with the MEG-3 IDR.
source: Like MEG-3, GCNA family members contain long N-terminal disordered domains, but these do not share sequence homology with the MEG-3 IDR (Carmell et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited sequence analysis.

claim: The MEG-3 C-terminus is the primary driver of MEG-3 condensation in zygotes.
source: The MEG-3 C-terminus is the primary driver of MEG-3 condensation in zygotes
evidence: This is supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: MEG-3Cterm (aa545–862) does not enrich asymmetrically in the cytoplasm but forms condensates in the zygote posterior and continues to form condensates only in P blastomeres despite being present in the cytoplasm of all cells.
source: MEG-3Cterm did not enrich asymmetrically in the cytoplasm but formed condensates in the zygote posterior and continued to form condensates only in P blastomeres despite being present in the cytoplasm of all cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MEG-3IDR (aa1–544) enriches in posterior cytoplasm and segregates preferentially to P blastomeres but does not appear robustly in condensates until the four-cell stage.
source: MEG-3IDR enriched in posterior cytoplasm and segregated preferentially to P blastomeres but did not appear robustly in condensates until the four-cell stage (P2 blastomere, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MEG-3698 behaves identically to MEG-3IDR.
source: MEG-3698 behaved identically to MEG-3IDR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MEG-3HMGL- behaves most similarly to wild-type MEG-3 enriching in the zygote posterior and forming condensates as early as the one-cell stage, although the condensates appear smaller at all stages.
source: MEG-3HMGL- behaved most similarly to wild-type MEG-3 enriching in the zygote posterior and forming condensates as early as the one-cell stage, although the condensates appeared smaller at all stages (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Wild-type MEG-3 and MEG-3HMGL- form a similar number of condensates at the four-cell stage.
source: Wild-type MEG-3 and MEG-3HMGL- formed a similar number of condensates, while MEG-3Cterm formed fewer and MEG-3IDR the least in the four-cell stage (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2B.

claim: MEG-3Cterm does not enrich in the P2 blastomere, whereas MEG-3IDR and MEG-3HMGL- enrich as efficiently as wild-type.
source: The MEG-3Cterm did not enrich in the P2 blastomere, whereas MEG-3IDR and MEG-3HMGL- enriched as efficiently as wild-type (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2C.

claim: None of the MEG-3 derivatives enrich in condensates as efficiently as wild-type.
source: Finally, none of MEG-3 derivatives enriched in condensates as efficiently as wild-type (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claim: After the four-cell stage, the low levels of wild-type MEG-3 and MEG-3HMGL- inherited by somatic blastomeres are rapidly cleared.
source: After the four-cell stage, the low levels of wild-type MEG-3 and MEG-3HMGL- inherited by somatic blastomeres were rapidly cleared.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MEG-3IDR and MEG-3Cterm persist in somatic blastomeres at least until the 28-cell stage.
source: In contrast, MEG-3IDR and MEG-3Cterm persisted in somatic blastomeres at least until the 28-cell stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MEG-3 and MEG-3HMGL- accumulate to similar levels, whereas MEG-3IDR and MEG-3Cterm are more abundant in mixed-stage embryo lysates.
source: Western analyses revealed that MEG-3 and MEG-3HMGL- accumulate to similar levels, whereas MEG-3IDR and MEG-3Cterm were more abundant in mixed-stage embryo lysates, consistent with slower turnover in somatic lineages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The MEG-3 IDR is necessary and sufficient for enrichment of cytoplasmic MEG-3 in germ plasm.
source: From this analysis, we conclude that (1) the MEG-3 IDR is necessary and sufficient for enrichment of cytoplasmic MEG-3 in germ plasm
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The MEG-3 C-terminus is necessary and sufficient to assemble MEG-3 condensates in germ plasm starting in the zygote stage.
source: (2) the MEG-3 C-terminus is necessary and sufficient to assemble MEG-3 condensates in germ plasm starting in the zygote stage
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The HMG-like motif enhances, but is not essential for, condensation.
source: (3) the HMG-like motif enhances, but is not essential for, condensation
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Both the C-terminus and the IDR are required for timely turnover of MEG-3 in somatic lineages.
source: (4) both the C-terminus and the IDR are required for timely turnover of MEG-3 in somatic lineages.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: MEG-3 and MEG-4 are required redundantly to localize PGL condensates to the posterior of the zygote for preferential segregation to the P lineage.
source: MEG-3 and MEG-4 are required redundantly to localize PGL condensates to the posterior of the zygote for preferential segregation to the P lineage (Smith et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited genetic studies.

claim: In embryos expressing wild-type MEG-3, MEG-3 and PGL-3 co-localize in posterior condensates that are segregated to the P1 blastomere.
source: In embryos expressing wild-type MEG-3, MEG-3 and PGL-3 co-localize in posterior condensates that are segregated to the P1 blastomere (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In embryos lacking meg-3 and meg-4, PGL-3 condensates distribute throughout the cytoplasm of the zygote and segregate equally to AB and P1.
source: In embryos lacking meg-3 and meg-4, PGL-3 condensates distributed throughout the cytoplasm of the zygote and segregated equally to AB and P1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Embryos expressing MEG-3IDR, MEG-3698, and MEG-3HMGL- fail to localize PGL condensates.
source: We observed a similar pattern in embryos expressing MEG-3IDR, MEG-3698, and MEG-3HMGL- indicating that none of these MEG-3 derivatives are sufficient to localize PGL condensates (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In embryos expressing MEG-3Cterm, PGL-3 condensates preferentially assemble in P1, although they are smaller and fewer than in wild-type.
source: In contrast, in embryos expressing MEG-3Cterm, PGL-3 condensates preferentially assembled in P1, although they were smaller and fewer than in wild-type (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: Embryos expressing MEG-3Cterm enrich PGL-3 in P1, though not as efficiently as wild-type.
source: Embryos expressing MEG-3Cterm enriches PGL-3 in P1, though not as efficiently as wild-type, while PGL-3 is not enriched in meg-3 meg-4, or embryos expressing MEG-3IDR or MEG-3HMGL- (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3C.

claim: PGL-3 is not enriched in meg-3 meg-4, or embryos expressing MEG-3IDR or MEG-3HMGL-.
source: Embryos expressing MEG-3Cterm enriches PGL-3 in P1, though not as efficiently as wild-type, while PGL-3 is not enriched in meg-3 meg-4, or embryos expressing MEG-3IDR or MEG-3HMGL- (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In wild-type 28-cell stage embryos, PGL-3 condensates are highly enriched in P4.
source: In wild-type 28-cell stage embryos, PGL-3 condensates are highly enriched in P4.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No enrichment of PGL-3 in P4 is observed in embryos expressing the MEG-3Cterm or any other MEG-3 variant.
source: No such enrichment was observed in embryos expressing the MEG-3Cterm or any other MEG-3 variant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The MEG-3Cterm is sufficient to enrich PGL-3 condensates in P blastomeres in early stages, but not sufficient to support robust PGL-3 localization through P4.
source: We conclude that the MEG-3Cterm is sufficient to enrich PGL-3 condensates in P blastomeres in early stages, but not sufficient to support robust PGL-3 localization through P4.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the data shown in Figures 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: PGL-3 condensates co-localize with MEG-3Cterm condensates (37/37 PGL-3 condensates scored in P1).
source: We found that PGL-3 condensates co-localized with MEG-3Cterm condensates (37/37 PGL-3 condensates scored in P1; Figure 3B) as in wild-type.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No co-localization of PGL-3 with MEG-3IDR or MEG-3HMGL- is observed.
source: In contrast, we observed no such co-localization with MEG-3IDR or MEG-3HMGL-.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: MEG-3IDR is mostly cytoplasmic and forms only rare condensates in P1.
source: The MEG-3IDR is mostly cytoplasmic and forms only rare condensates in P1.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PGL condensates occasionally have an adjacent MEG-3IDR condensate (5/19 PGL-3 condensates scored in P1), but these are not co-localized.
source: We occasionally observed PGL condensates with an adjacent MEG-3IDR condensate (5/19 PGL-3 condensates scored in P1, Figure 3B), but these were not co-localized.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: MEG-3HMGL- forms many condensates in P1, although these tend to be smaller than wild-type.
source: Unlike the MEG-3IDR, MEG-3HMGL- forms many condensates in P1, although these tended to be smaller than wild-type (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: PGL condensates occasionally have an adjacent MEG-3HMGL- condensate (12/30 PGL-3 condensates scored in P1), but fully overlapping PGL/MEG-3HMGL- co-condensates are never observed.
source: Still, although we occasionally observed PGL condensates with an adjacent MEG-3HMGL- condensate (12/30 PGL-3 condensates scored in P1; Figure 3B), we never observed fully overlapping PGL/MEG-3HMGL- co-condensates.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Despite forming many condensates in P blastomeres, MEG-3HMGL- condensates do not associate efficiently with, and do not support the localization of, PGL-3 condensates.
source: We conclude that, despite forming many condensates in P blastomeres, MEG-3HMGL- condensates do not associate efficiently with, and do not support the localization of, PGL-3 condensates.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: MEG-3 recruits mRNAs to P granules by direct binding that traps mRNA into the non-dynamic MEG-3 condensates.
source: MEG-3 recruits mRNAs to P granules by direct binding that traps mRNA into the non-dynamic MEG-3 condensates (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Prior to polarization, Y51F10.2 is uniformly distributed throughout the zygote cytoplasm.
source: Prior to polarization, Y51F10.2 is uniformly distributed throughout the zygote cytoplasm (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Y51F10.2 becomes progressively enriched in P granules starting in the late one-cell stage and forms easily detectable micron-sized foci by the four-cell stage.
source: Y51F10.2 becomes progressively enriched in P granules starting in the late one-cell stage and forms easily detectable micron-sized foci by the four-cell stage (Lee et al., 2020; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A and cited studies.

claim: In meg-3 meg-4 embryos, Y51F10.2 remains uniformly distributed in the cytoplasm at all stages.
source: In contrast, in meg-3 meg-4 embryos, Y51F10.2 remains uniformly distributed in the cytoplasm at all stages.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Embryos expressing MEG-3IDR, MEG-3Cterm, and MEG-3HMGL- fail to assemble Y51F10.2 foci.
source: Strikingly, we observed the same failure to assemble Y51F10.2 foci in embryos expressing MEG-3IDR, MEG-3Cterm, and MEG-3HMGL- (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In wild-type, Y51F10.2 RNA levels do not change significantly from the one-cell to the four-cell stage.
source: In wild-type, Y51F10.2 RNA levels do not change significantly from the one-cell to the four-cell stage.
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In meg-3 meg-4 embryos, Y51F10.2 levels decrease by ~50% by the four-cell stage, despite starting at levels similar to wild-type in the one-cell stage.
source: In contrast, in meg-3 meg-4 embryos, Y51F10.2 levels decreased by ~50% by the four-cell stage, despite starting at levels similar to wild-type in the one-cell stage.
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A similar loss of Y51F10.2 RNA is observed in embryos expressing MEG-3IDR, MEG-3Cterm, and MEG-3HMGL-.
source: We observed a similar loss of Y51F10.2 RNA in embryos expressing MEG-3IDR, MEG-3Cterm, and MEG-3HMGL- (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4B.

claim: nos-2 levels remain constant from the one-cell to four-cell stage in embryos expressing wild-type MEG-3, and decrease in meg-3 meg-4 embryos and embryos expressing MEG-3IDR, MEG-3Cterm, and MEG-3HMGL-.
source: Similar to Y51F10.2, nos-2 levels remained constant from the one-cell to four-cell stage in embryos expressing wild-type MEG-3, and decreased in meg-3 meg-4 embryos and embryos expressing MEG-3IDR, MEG-3Cterm, and MEG-3HMGL- (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Failure to recruit Y51F10.2 and nos-2 mRNAs into granules leads to their premature degradation.
source: These results suggest that failure to recruit Y51F10.2 and nos-2 mRNAs into granules leads to their premature degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mRNA levels decrease when not recruited to granules.

claim: At the four-cell stage, Y51F10.2 mRNA levels are approximately twofold higher in P2 than in somatic blastomeres in wild-type embryos.
source: At the four-cell stage, Y51F10.2 mRNA levels were approximately twofold higher P2 than in somatic blastomeres in wild-type embryos, and ~1.2-fold higher in meg-3 meg-4 embryos and in embryos expressing MEG-3IDR, MEG-3Cterm, and MEG-3HMGL- (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4C.

claim: At the four-cell stage, Y51F10.2 mRNA levels are ~1.2-fold higher in P2 than in somatic blastomeres in meg-3 meg-4 embryos and in embryos expressing MEG-3IDR, MEG-3Cterm, and MEG-3HMGL-.
source: At the four-cell stage, Y51F10.2 mRNA levels were approximately twofold higher P2 than in somatic blastomeres in wild-type embryos, and ~1.2-fold higher in meg-3 meg-4 embryos and in embryos expressing MEG-3IDR, MEG-3Cterm, and MEG-3HMGL- (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4C.

claim: By the 28-cell stage, in wild-type embryos, Y51F10.2 levels are ~10-fold higher in the germline founder cell P4 compared to somatic blastomeres.
source: By the 28-cell stage, in wild-type embryos, Y51F10.2 levels were ~10-fold higher in the germline founder cell P4 compared to somatic blastomeres.
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In meg-3 meg-4 embryos, Y51F10.2 mRNA levels are only approximately twofold enriched over somatic levels at the 28-cell stage.
source: In contrast, in meg-3 meg-4 embryos, Y51F10.2 mRNA levels were only approximately twofold enriched over somatic levels.
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In embryos expressing the MEG-3IDR, MEG-3Cterm, and MEG-3HMGL-, Y51F10.2 enrichment in P4 averages around approximately twofold.
source: Similarly, in embryos expressing the MEG-3IDR, MEG-3Cterm, and MEG-3HMGL-, Y51F10.2 enrichment in P4 averaged around approximately twofold (Figure 4A, D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In wild-type 28-cell stage embryos, poly-A signal intensity in P4 is ~1.8-fold higher than that observed in somatic blastomeres.
source: In wild-type 28-cell stage embryos, a concentrated poly-A signal is detected around the nucleus of the P4 blastomere. Poly-A signal intensity in P4 is ~1.8-fold higher than that observed in somatic blastomeres (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This is supported by oligo-dT in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: Poly-A enrichment in P4 is not detected in meg-3 meg-4 mutants.
source: This enrichment was not detected in meg-3 meg-4 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by oligo-dT in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: In meg-3 meg-4 mutants, and in embryos expressing the three MEG-3 derivatives, poly-A signal intensity is similar between the somatic and P4 blastomeres.
source: In meg-3 meg-4 mutants, and in embryos expressing the three MEG-3 derivatives, poly-A signal intensity was similar between the somatic and P4 blastomeres.
evidence: This is supported by oligo-dT in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: Failure to efficiently segregate and stabilize maternal mRNAs in P blastomeres has been linked to the partial penetrance maternal-effect sterility (~30%) of meg-3 meg-4 mutants.
source: Failure to efficiently segregate and stabilize maternal mRNAs in P blastomeres has been linked to the partial penetrance maternal-effect sterility (~30%) of meg-3 meg-4 mutants (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited genetic studies.

claim: Similar levels of sterility (~30%) are observed in hermaphrodites derived from mothers expressing the MEG-3IDR, MEG-3Cterm, and MEG-3HMGL-.
source: We observed similar levels of sterility in hermaphrodites derived from mothers expressing the MEG-3IDR, MEG-3Cterm, and MEG-3HMGL- (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by sterility assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The MEG-3 C-terminus, IDR, and HMG-like motif are all required for efficient mRNA recruitment to P granules.
source: We conclude that the MEG-3 C-terminus, IDR, and HMG-like motif are all required for efficient mRNA recruitment to P granules, which in turn is required for enrichment and stabilization in the P lineage and robust germ cell fate specification.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Efficient mRNA recruitment to P granules is required for enrichment and stabilization in the P lineage and robust germ cell fate specification.
source: We conclude that the MEG-3 C-terminus, IDR, and HMG-like motif are all required for efficient mRNA recruitment to P granules, which in turn is required for enrichment and stabilization in the P lineage and robust germ cell fate specification.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: MEG-3 readily condenses with RNA in vitro.
source: We showed previously that MEG-3 readily condenses with RNA in vitro (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited in vitro studies.

claim: The MEG-3 IDR binds an RNA oligo (poly-U(30)) with near nanomolar affinity in vitro.
source: Using fluorescence polarization and gel shift assays, we previously showed that the MEG-3 IDR binds an RNA oligo (poly-U(30)) with near nanomolar affinity in vitro (Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited binding assays.

claim: MEG-3IDR and MEG-3698 exhibit high affinity for poly-U(30).
source: Consistent with previous observations (Smith et al., 2016), we found that MEG-3IDR and MEG-3698 exhibit high affinity for poly-U(30) (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by filter binding assay data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Wild-type MEG-3 binds poly-U(30) efficiently albeit at a lower affinity compared to MEG-3IDR and MEG-3698.
source: Wild-type MEG-3 also bound poly-U(30) efficiently albeit at a lower affinity compared to MEG-3IDR and MEG-3698.
evidence: This is supported by filter binding assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: MEG-3Cterm exhibits negligible RNA binding.
source: In contrast, MEG-3Cterm exhibited negligible RNA binding (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by filter binding assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The HMGL motif does not contribute to RNA binding in MEG-3.
source: MEG-3HMGL- bound to RNA as efficiently as full-length MEG-3, indicating that the HMGL motif does not contribute to RNA binding in MEG-3 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by filter binding assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Full-length MEG-3 and MEG-3IDR bind to nos-2 RNA with the same high affinity.
source: The competition assay revealed that full-length MEG-3 and MEG-3IDR bind to nos-2 RNA with the same high affinity.
evidence: This is supported by competition binding assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The MEG-3 IDR is necessary and sufficient for RNA binding.
source: We conclude that the MEG-3 IDR is necessary and sufficient for RNA binding.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the binding assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: MEG-3 condensation is sensitive to salt and RNA concentration with RNA having a strong solubilizing influence especially in low salt.
source: MEG-3 condensation is sensitive to salt and RNA concentration with RNA having a strong solubilizing influence especially in low salt (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited in vitro condensation studies.

claim: At 150 nM MEG-3 in low salt/high RNA condensation buffer (50 mM NaCl to 80 ng/μL nos-2 RNA), MEG-3 and variants are all soluble.
source: At that concentration, MEG-3 and variants were all soluble in low salt/high RNA condensation buffer (50 mM NaCl to 80 ng/μL nos-2 RNA) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro condensation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Under higher salt conditions (150 mM NaCl salt and 20 ng/μL or 80 ng/μL nos-2 RNA), MEG-3IDR and MEG-3698 remain mostly soluble forming only rare condensates.
source: Under higher salt conditions (150 mM NaCl salt and 20 ng/μL or 80 ng/μL nos-2 RNA), MEG-3IDR and MEG-3698 remained mostly soluble forming only rare condensates (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplements 1, 2).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro condensation data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplements 1, 2.

claim: Under higher salt conditions (150 mM NaCl salt and 20 ng/μL or 80 ng/μL nos-2 RNA), full-length MEG-3 forms robust condensates.
source: In contrast, full-length MEG-3 formed robust condensates under those conditions.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro condensation data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: MEG-3C-term forms condensates, albeit with lower efficiency compared to MEG-3.
source: MEG-3C-term also formed condensates, albeit with lower efficiency compared to MEG-3 (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro condensation data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The MEG-3Cterm condensates are approximately twofold less efficient at recruiting RNA compared to full-length MEG-3 and MEG-3IDR.
source: The MEG-3Cterm condensates were also approximately twofold less efficient at recruiting RNA compared to full-length MEG-3 and MEG-3IDR (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro condensation data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: As observed in vivo, the C-terminus is the primary driver of MEG-3 condensation in vitro.
source: We conclude that, as observed in vivo, the C-terminus is the primary driver of MEG-3 condensation.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the in vitro condensation data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The MEG-3 C-terminus is not sufficient for maximum condensation or RNA recruitment, which additionally require the IDR.
source: The MEG-3 C-terminus is not sufficient, however, for maximum condensation or RNA recruitment, which additionally require the IDR.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the in vitro condensation data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Under all in vitro conditions tested, MEG-3HMGL- and MEG-3CtermHMGL- behave identically to MEG-3 and MEG-3Cterm, respectively.
source: Surprisingly, under all conditions, MEG-3HMGL- and MEG-3CtermHMGL- behaved identically to MEG-3 and MEG-3Cterm, respectively (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that the HMGL motif is dispensable for RNA recruitment and condensation in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro condensation data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The HMGL motif is dispensable for RNA recruitment and condensation in vitro.
source: Surprisingly, under all conditions, MEG-3HMGL- and MEG-3CtermHMGL- behaved identically to MEG-3 and MEG-3Cterm, respectively (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that the HMGL motif is dispensable for RNA recruitment and condensation in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro condensation data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: HMGL is required for RNA recruitment and efficient condensation in vivo, suggesting that in vitro conditions do not fully reproduce in vivo conditions.
source: HMGL was required for RNA recruitment and efficient condensation in vivo (Figure 4), suggesting that our in vitro conditions do not fully reproduce in vivo conditions (see below).
evidence: This is inferred by comparing in vivo and in vitro results.

claim: When combined in condensation buffer, MEG-3 and PGL-3 form co-condensates that resemble the architecture of P granules in vivo, with the smaller MEG-3 condensates (~100 nm) forming a dense layer on the surface of the larger PGL-3 condensates.
source: When combined in condensation buffer, MEG-3 and PGL-3 form co-condensates that resemble the architecture of P granules in vivo, with the smaller MEG-3 condensates (~100 nm) forming a dense layer on the surface of the larger PGL-3 condensates (Putnam et al., 2019; Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro co-condensation data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, and cited studies.

claim: The MEG-3Cterm forms co-condensates with PGL-3 that are indistinguishable from those formed by wild-type MEG-3.
source: We found that the MEG-3Cterm formed co-condensates with PGL-3 that were indistinguishable from those formed by wild-type MEG-3 (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro co-condensation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: The MEG-3IDR mixes homogenously with the PGL-3 phase.
source: The MEG-3IDR, in contrast, mixed homogenously with the PGL-3 phase as previously reported (Putnam et al., 2019, Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro co-condensation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and cited studies.

claim: MEG-3HMGL- and MEG-3CtermHMGL- behave as MEG-3 and MEG-3Cterm, respectively, in in vitro co-condensation assays.
source: MEG-3HMGL- and MEG-3CtermHMGL- behaved as MEG-3 and MEG-3Cterm, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro co-condensation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: In vivo, MEG-3HMGL- does not associate efficiently with PGL-3 condensates, suggesting that in vitro conditions do not reproduce the more stringent in vivo environment.
source: In vivo, MEG-3HMGL- does not associate efficiently with PGL-3 condensates (Figure 3B), again suggesting that in vitro conditions do not reproduce the more stringent in vivo environment.
evidence: This is inferred by comparing in vivo and in vitro results.

claim: In the absence of RNA, MEG-3 and PGL-3 form co-condensates that are indistinguishable from co-condensates assembled in the presence of RNA.
source: Under these conditions, MEG-3 and PGL-3 formed co-condensates that were indistinguishable from co-condensates assembled in the presence of RNA (compare right and left panels, Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro co-condensation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: The C-terminus is necessary and sufficient for co-assembly of MEG-3 and PGL-3 condensates in vitro.
source: Again, the C-terminus was necessary and sufficient for co-assembly.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the in vitro co-condensation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: MEG-3IDR homogenously mixes with the PGL-3 phase and does not form independent condensates in the absence of RNA.
source: MEG-3IDR homogenously mixed with the PGL-3 phase and did not form independent condensates.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro co-condensation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Condensation of MEG-3 on the surface of PGL condensates requires the MEG-3 C-terminus and does not require RNA in vitro.
source: We conclude that condensation of MEG-3 on the surface of PGL condensates requires the MEG-3 C-terminus and does not require RNA in vitro.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the in vitro co-condensation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Under high RNA conditions (40 ng/μL labeled nos-2 RNA and unlabeled 150 μM poly-U(30)), all MEG-3 variants are recruited to PGL condensates.
source: Under these high RNA conditions, all variants were recruited to PGL condensates, but only full-length MEG-3 (and MEG-3HMGL-) formed a distinctive layer around PGL condensates that recruited RNA above the background level recruited to the PGL-3 phase (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro co-condensation data shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: Only full-length MEG-3 (and MEG-3HMGL-) form a distinctive layer around PGL condensates that recruits RNA above the background level recruited to the PGL-3 phase.
source: Under these high RNA conditions, all variants were recruited to PGL condensates, but only full-length MEG-3 (and MEG-3HMGL-) formed a distinctive layer around PGL condensates that recruited RNA above the background level recruited to the PGL-3 phase (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro co-condensation data shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: MEG-3IDR and MEG-3Cterm mix with the PGL phase and do not enrich nos-2 RNA above background levels.
source: MEG-3IDR and MEG-3Cterm, in contrast, mixed with the PGL phase and did not enrich nos-2 RNA above background levels (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro co-condensation data shown in Figure 6B, C.

claim: Enrichment of nos-2 RNA in MEG-3/PGL-3 co-condensates requires robust MEG-3 condensation driven by the combined action of the MEG-3 IDR and C-terminus.
source: These observations suggest that enrichment of nos-2 RNA in MEG-3/PGL-3 co-condensates requires robust MEG-3 condensation driven by the combined action of the MEG-3 IDR and C-terminus.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro co-condensation data shown in Figure 6.

claim: MEG-3 binds directly to PGL-1, as determined in a GST-pull-down assay using partially purified recombinant proteins.
source: We reported previously that MEG-3 binds directly to PGL-1, as determined in a GST-pull-down assay using partially purified recombinant proteins (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited GST pull-down assays.

claim: GST::MEG-3Cterm binds efficiently to PGL-1 and PGL-3, but not to MBP or to an unrelated control protein PAA-1.
source: We found that the GST::MEG-3Cterm binds efficiently to PGL-1 and PGL-3, but not to MBP or to an unrelated control protein PAA-1 (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 7A, B.

claim: A GST::MEG-3Cterm fusion with mutations in the HMG-like domain binds less efficiently to both PGL-1 and PGL-3.
source: A GST::MEG-3Cterm fusion with mutations in the HMG-like domain bound less efficiently to both PGL-1 and PGL-3 (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 7A, B.

claim: PGL-3 is recruited efficiently to beads coated with MEG-3C-term, but not to beads coated with MEG-3IDR or MEG-3Cterm HMGL-.
source: We found that PGL-3 is recruited efficiently to beads coated with MEG-3C-term, but not to beads coated with MEG-3IDR or MEG-3Cterm HMGL- (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by bead halo assay data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The MEG-3C-term binds directly to PGL-3 and this interaction requires the HMGL motif.
source: We conclude that the MEG-3C-term binds directly to PGL-3 and that this interaction requires the HMGL motif.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the GST pull-down and bead halo assay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Direct binding between MEG-3 and PGL-3 molecules may be necessary to assemble co-condensates in the crowded in vivo environment and may not be required in vitro where no other proteins or condensates compete for binding to MEG-3 or PGL-3.
source: This finding provides a potential explanation for why the HMGL is required for co-assembly of MEG-3 and PGL-3 condensates in vivo but not in vitro. Direct binding between MEG-3 and PGL-3 molecules may be necessary to assemble co-condensates in the crowded in vivo environment and may not be required in vitro where no other proteins or condensates compete for binding to MEG-3 or PGL-3.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Binding between PGL-3 and MEG-3 recruits MEG-3 to the surface of PGL-3 condensates in germ plasm and stimulates condensation of MEG-3 and MEG-3-bound RNAs.
source: These findings (summarized in Figure 8) combined with prior analyses (Putnam et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2020) suggest the following model for P granule assembly: binding between PGL-3 and MEG-3 recruits MEG-3 to the surface of PGL-3 condensates in germ plasm and stimulates condensation of MEG-3 and MEG-3-bound RNAs.
evidence: This is a model inferred from the experimental data in the manuscript and cited studies.

claim: The MEG-3 layer protects mRNAs from degradation and stabilizes PGL-3 condensates in germ plasm ensuring their preferential segregation to the germline founder cell P4.
source: The MEG-3 layer protects mRNAs from degradation and stabilizes PGL-3 condensates in germ plasm ensuring their preferential segregation to the germline founder cell P4.
evidence: This is a model inferred from the experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Assembly of MEG-3/PGL-3 co-condensates depends on the MEG-3 C-terminus and HMGL domain and does not require RNA.
source: Assembly of MEG-3/PGL-3 co-condensates depends on the MEG-3 C-terminus and HMGL domain and does not require RNA
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The MEG-3 C-terminus contains an HMG-like motif required to bind to PGL-3 and additional predicted low-disorder sequences that drive condensation by an unknown mechanism.
source: The MEG-3 C-terminus contains an HMG-like motif required to bind to PGL-3 and additional predicted low-disorder sequences that drive condensation by an unknown mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and structural predictions.

claim: The HMGL domain is not required for condensation in vitro but is required for maximal condensation efficiency in vivo.
source: The HMGL domain is not required for condensation in vitro but is required for maximal condensation efficiency in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by comparing in vitro and in vivo data shown in Figures 2 and 6.

claim: The HMGL domain enhances condensation indirectly in vivo by concentrating MEG-3 on the surface of PGL droplets, which stimulates condensation.
source: We suggest the HMGL domain enhances condensation indirectly in vivo by concentrating MEG-3 on the surface of PGL droplets, which stimulates condensation (Putnam et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism inferred from the experimental data and cited studies.

claim: Docking of P bodies on stress granules has been proposed to involve RNA:RNA duplexes.
source: Docking of P bodies on stress granules has been proposed to involve RNA:RNA duplexes (Tauber et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Docking of MEG-3 condensates on PGL condensates does not require RNA in vitro and can occur in the absence of any visible RNA enrichment in vivo.
source: In contrast, we find that docking of MEG-3 condensates on PGL condensates does not require RNA in vitro and can occur in the absence of any visible RNA enrichment in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 6.

claim: Mutations in the HMGL domain that prevent binding between MEG-3 and PGL-3 molecules in solution prevent docking of MEG-3 and PGL condensates in vivo.
source: Most strikingly, mutations in the HMGL domain that prevent binding between MEG-3 and PGL-3 molecules in solution prevent docking of MEG-3 and PGL condensates in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 7.

claim: MEG-3 condensation and co-assembly with PGL-3 condensates is driven primarily by protein-protein interactions and does not require RNA.
source: Together, these observations suggest that MEG-3 condensation and co-assembly with PGL-3 condensates is driven primarily by protein-protein interactions and does not require RNA.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figures 3, 6, and 7.

claim: The HMGL domain is dispensable for co-assembly of MEG-3 and PGL-3 condensates in vitro, indicating that the condensation assay conditions do not fully reproduce the stringent environment of the cytoplasm.
source: We note that the HMGL domain is dispensable for co-assembly of MEG-3 and PGL-3 condensates in vitro, indicating that our condensation assay conditions do not fully reproduce the stringent environment of the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is inferred by comparing in vitro and in vivo results.

claim: Enrichment of PGL droplets to the posterior of the zygote requires meg-3.
source: We previously reported that enrichment of PGL droplets to the posterior of the zygote requires meg-3 (Smith et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited genetic studies.

claim: MEG-3's ability to localize PGL is linked to MEG-3's ability to associate stably with the PGL interface.
source: Our new findings suggest that this activity is linked to MEG-3's ability to associate stably with the PGL interface.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: MEG-3Cterm, which is sufficient for MEG-3/PGL co-assembly, is sufficient to localize PGL in zygotes.
source: MEG-3Cterm, which is sufficient for MEG-3/PGL co-assembly, is sufficient to localize PGL in zygotes.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: MEG-3HMGL- condensates, which do not interact stably with PGL condensates, fail to enrich PGL condensates in the posterior of zygotes.
source: Conversely, MEG-3HMGL- condensates, which do not interact stably with PGL condensates, fail to enrich PGL condensates in the posterior of zygotes.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: PGL localization involves preferential growth and dissolution of PGL droplets in the anterior and posterior, respectively.
source: PGL localization involves preferential growth and dissolution of PGL droplets in the anterior and posterior, respectively.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from cited studies.

claim: Tight binding of MEG condensates may lower the surface tension of PGL droplets allowing MEG/PGL co-assemblies in the posterior to grow at the expense of the less stable, 'naked' PGL droplets in the anterior.
source: One possibility is that tight binding of MEG condensates lowers the surface tension of PGL droplets allowing MEG/PGL co-assemblies in the posterior to grow at the expense of the less stable, 'naked' PGL droplets in the anterior.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the observations.

claim: MEG-3 asymmetry is driven by a competition for RNA between the MEG-3 IDR and MEX-5, an RNA-binding protein that acts as an RNA sink in the anterior.
source: We previously hypothesized that MEG-3 asymmetry is driven by a competition for RNA between the MEG-3 IDR and MEX-5, an RNA-binding protein that acts as an RNA sink in the anterior (Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from cited previous work.

claim: The MEG-3 IDR is sufficient to enrich MEG-3 in posterior cytoplasm.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the MEG-3 IDR is sufficient to enrich MEG-3 in posterior cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The MEG-3Cterm condenses preferentially in the zygote posterior despite uniform distribution in the cytoplasm, suggesting that additional mechanisms acting on the MEG-3 C-terminus contribute to MEG-3 regulation in space.
source: Unexpectedly, however, we found that the MEG-3Cterm condenses preferentially in the zygote posterior despite uniform distribution in the cytoplasm, suggesting that additional mechanisms acting on the MEG-3 C-terminus contribute to MEG-3 regulation in space.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A recent study examining MEG-3 dynamics by single-molecule imaging found that the slowly diffusing MEG-3 molecules that populate the MEG-3 gradient in the cytoplasm represent a distinct population of MEG-3 molecules from those that associate with PGL droplets.
source: Consistent with this view, a recent study examining MEG-3 dynamics by single-molecule imaging (Wu et al., 2019) found that the slowly diffusing MEG-3 molecules that populate the MEG-3 gradient in the cytoplasm represent a distinct population of MEG-3 molecules from those that associate with PGL droplets.
evidence: This is supported by cited single-molecule imaging studies.

claim: MEG-3 asymmetry is sustained by two independent mechanisms: one acting on the MEG-3 C-terminus that biases condensation of MEG-3 in posterior cytoplasm and one acting on the MEG-3 IDR that enriches MEG-3 molecules in posterior cytoplasm.
source: We propose that MEG-3 asymmetry is sustained by two independent mechanisms: one acting on the MEG-3 C-terminus that biases condensation of MEG-3 in posterior cytoplasm and one acting on the MEG-3 IDR that enriches MEG-3 molecules in posterior cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a proposed model inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The mechanism acting on the MEG-3 IDR may serve to segregate high levels of MEG-3 to P blastomeres needed to support PGL asymmetry through the P4 stage.
source: We speculate that the latter may serve to segregate high levels of MEG-3 to P blastomeres needed to support PGL asymmetry through the P4 stage.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observations.

claim: The MEG-3Cterm, which does not enrich in a gradient, is not sufficient to localize PGL condensates in P blastomeres past the four-cell stage.
source: Consistent with this view, the MEG-3Cterm, which does not enrich in a gradient, is not sufficient to localize PGL condensates in P blastomeres past the four-cell stage.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The MEG-3 IDR binds RNA with high-affinity in vitro but is not sufficient to enrich RNA in vivo despite forming some condensates.
source: The MEG-3 IDR binds RNA with high-affinity in vitro but is not sufficient to enrich RNA in vivo despite forming some condensates.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: RNA recruitment in vivo additionally requires the MEG-3 C-terminus including the HMG-like motif.
source: RNA recruitment in vivo additionally requires the MEG-3 C-terminus including the HMG-like motif.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Maximal MEG-3 condensation is essential to build a protein scaffold that can support stable RNA recruitment in vivo.
source: These observations suggest that maximal MEG-3 condensation is essential to build a protein scaffold that can support stable RNA recruitment in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: Separate domains for RNA-binding and protein condensation have also been observed for other germ granule scaffolds.
source: Separate domains for RNA-binding and protein condensation have also been observed for other germ granule scaffolds.
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on other germ granule proteins.

claim: The Balbiani body protein Xvelo uses a prion-like domain to aggregate and a separate RNA-binding domain to recruit RNA.
source: For example, the Balbiani body protein Xvelo uses a prion-like domain to aggregate and a separate RNA-binding domain to recruit RNA (Boke et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on Xvelo.

claim: Condensation of Drosophila Oskar does not require the predicted Oskar RNA-binding domain, although this domain augments condensation.
source: Similarly, condensation of Drosophila Oskar does not require the predicted Oskar RNA-binding domain, although this domain augments condensation (Kistler et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on Oskar.

claim: Condensation of G3BP in vitro requires RNA and two C-terminal RNA-binding domains.
source: Condensation of G3BP in vitro requires RNA and two C-terminal RNA-binding domains.
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on G3BP.

claim: A N-terminal dimerization domain in G3BP is required but, unlike the prion-like domain of Xvelo or the C-terminus of MEG-3, is not sufficient to drive condensation on its own.
source: A N-terminal dimerization domain is also required but, unlike the prion-like domain of Xvelo or the C-terminus of MEG-3, is not sufficient to drive condensation on its own.
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on G3BP.

claim: Dimerization of G3BP is thought to enhance LLPS indirectly by augmenting the RNA-binding valency of G3BP complexes.
source: Dimerization of G3BP is thought to enhance LLPS indirectly by augmenting the RNA-binding valency of G3BP complexes.
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on G3BP.

claim: G3BP contains an inhibitory domain that gates its RNA-binding activity and condensation at low RNA concentrations.
source: G3BP also contains an inhibitory domain that gates its RNA-binding activity and condensation at low RNA concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on G3BP.

claim: The modular organization of G3BP ensures that G3BP functions as a sensitive switch that initiates LLPS when sufficient RNA molecules are available to cross-link G3BP dimers into a large network.
source: This modular organization ensures that G3BP functions as a sensitive switch that initiates LLPS when sufficient RNA molecules are available to cross-link G3BP dimers into a large network (Guillén-Boixet et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on G3BP.

claim: Stress granules are transient structures that form under conditions of general translational arrest where thousands of transcripts are released from ribosomes.
source: Stress granules are transient structures that form under conditions of general translational arrest where thousands of transcripts are released from ribosomes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about stress granules.

claim: Germ granules are long-lived structures that assemble in translationally active cytoplasm and recruit only a few hundred specific transcripts (~500 in C. elegans embryos).
source: In contrast, germ granules are long-lived structures that assemble in translationally active cytoplasm and recruit only a few hundred specific transcripts (~500 in C. elegans embryos) (Jamieson-Lucy and Mullins, 2019; Lee et al., 2020; Trcek and Lehmann, 2019; Updike and Strome, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on germ granules.

claim: Protein-based condensation mechanisms may be better suited to assemble long-lived granules able to capture and retain rare transcripts.
source: One possibility is that protein-based condensation mechanisms may be better suited to assemble long-lived granules able to capture and retain rare transcripts.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the differences between stress granules and germ granules.

claim: By concentrating IDRs with affinity for RNA, protein scaffolds could act as seeds for localized LLPS to amplify protein and RNA condensation.
source: By concentrating IDRs with affinity for RNA, protein scaffolds could act as seeds for localized LLPS to amplify protein and RNA condensation.

claim: IDRs undergo spontaneous LLPS in cells when artificially tethered to protein modules that self-assemble into large multimeric structures.
